To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have characterized 13 novel MLH1 alleles that are associated with hereditary non-poloypsis colon cancer and that the severity of the defect conferred by each allele is influenced by the genetic background of yeast cells in which the assay is performed.

we determined the MRR proficiency conferred by 28 mlh1 alleles of baker's yeasts that correspond to nontruncating human MLH1 missense mutations, and we observed that genetic background can affect the MMR proficiency of certain mlh1 alleles, which suggests that genetic background can influence the pathogenicity in humans of MMR mutations.
the majority of non-truncating MLH1 mutations are pathogenic, and that the genetic background of an individual can play an important part in determining the pathogenesis of certain MMR mutations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the function of the yeast MLH1 protein and how it relates to the function of the human protein.
a large-scale functional analysis of non-truncating MLH1 mutations and the role of genetic background on MMR function in yeast.
the study of the genetic background of human diseases and the development of a new method for studying genetic background effects in the context of a model organism.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
22 out of 28 MLH1 missense alleles are likely pathogenic, while six alleles are likely to be non-pathogenic.
all 28 MLH1 alleles tested in this study are likely to be associated with HNPCC.
all 15 of these alleles are likely to cause HNPCC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of missense mutations in the MLH1 gene, which have been reported as pathogenic in humans, are indeed likely to be pathologic in the yeast system.
the yeast assay provides a useful tool to determine the MMR proficiency of MLH1 variants, but the results may not be directly transferable to the human system.
the majority of non-truncating missense variants of MLH1 are pathogenic, but that genetic context may affect the degree to which these mutations are deleterious.
The main takeaway from our work is that
yeast functional assays, especially those that are more sensitive, can provide valuable information about the potential pathogenic effects of missense MLH1 mutations.
the genetic context in which a variant is studied can affect the conclusions drawn about the variant's pathogenicity.
the genetic background of a cell can affect the function of a mutant protein, and that this effect may be important in determining the clinical significance of a mutation.
